title: Women's rugby players fight to save team after Bishop's University cuts varsity program
summary: Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, Que., has decided to cut its women’s varsity rugby team. The news comes as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world, and university varsity teams are a…

image.caption: The Gaitors are the women's varsity rugby team at Bishop's University. The players were told this week that the school will be cutting its varsity status after this academic year is over. (Courtesy of Bronwyn Chénard)

blocks.text: Montreal

Bishop’s University in Sherbrooke, Que., has decided to cut its women’s varsity rugby team. The news comes as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world, and university varsity teams are a pipeline to fuel the national team roster.
Some players had moved across the country to join team, were blindsided by decision

Women’s rugby players at Bishop's University in Sherbrooke, Que., say they were left in tears and shock when they were told on Monday the team would no longer receive varsity support or funding beyond this school year.
According to the university, the decision was taken by its board of governors following a year-long review.
“It really felt like being stabbed in the chest,” said Tessa Brosseau, who moved from Vancouver to attend the university in Quebec’s Eastern Townships.
"The reason that I'm at Bishop's is because of Bishop's women's rugby,” said the fourth-year student. “It means everything. It means my life.”
Claudia Croteau and Abigail Burns, both rookies from Alberta, also moved across the country to play for the varsity rugby team.
Bishop’s University drops women's rugby and men's lacrosse — blindsiding athletes

The young women say they think of each other as family now, bonded together by all the hard work and sacrifices they've each made to be part of the team — including countless hours of training during early mornings, late nights and rainy practices.
Fighting to keep their rugby dreams alive
The school suggested the team could continue as a club. But the players don’t see that as an equivalent replacement.
“None of us came here to play club rugby,” said Brosseau. “We came here to potentially be prospects for the national program."

Universities with a varsity team can be a pipeline to get onto the national roster. The prospect of that is particularly appealing to young female athletes now, as Canada’s women’s rugby team ranks third in the world.
Being a varsity team means more amenities, as well, including access to coaching and medical staff. It's also the last level before being able to play professionally.

The players are not willing to let go of that dream without a fight.
They’ve launched an online petition that’s garnered more than 6,000 signatures, and are considering fundraising in hopes of reversing the board’s decision.
If a solution can’t be found, Croteau admitted that she and other rookies are contemplating transferring schools as a last resort, in order to be able to still play rugby at the varsity level.
“Yes, we love Bishop’s,” she said, “but what makes Bishop’s so amazing is rugby."
'Women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear'
In its explanation of the decision to cut the varsity program, the university acknowledged it was facing “significant financial pressure.”

However, the team says it was never consulted to help address that challenge. Nor has it been informed of what criteria was considered when taking the decision, which the university has said is final.
Rylee Fletcher, who’s in her fourth year at Bishop’s, is hoping to bring wider attention to what she calls a "devastating" decision.
“At a time when women’s sports are gaining long-overdue recognition, investment, and support, it is incredibly discouraging to see opportunities for female athletes being taken away,” she said.
“We believe women’s sports deserve to grow, not disappear.”
The team finished last this season, but the players believe the future of the team is still bright. (Courtesy of Bronwyn Chénard)
Bishop’s University has said the school has chosen to concentrate its resources on fewer varsity teams to better support their needs.

"This decision reflects financial and operational sustainability, competitive fit and the resources each sport requires. It does not diminish the value of women’s rugby or the people who play it," a school representative said in an emailed statement.
Bishop's plans to keep four women’s and four men’s varsity teams. They include both basketball and golf teams, as well as men’s football and rugby, and women’s hockey and soccer.
Men's lacrosse team also cut
In addition to Bishop's women's varsity rugby team, the men’s varsity lacrosse team has also been cut.

The Canadian University Field Lacrosse Association (CUFLA) said in a statement that it hasn't officially been notified of the decision, but considers it to be a "significant setback" to its efforts of reversing the trend of Canadian student athletes choosing American universities to pursue their education and lacrosse careers.

The CUFLA says it has noticed a "significant increase" in Canadian student athletes returning from universities in the U.S. over the past several years to continue their pursuits at Canadian institutions.
"Lacrosse is increasingly becoming a driver of university enrolment, making the decision by Bishop's University particularly difficult to understand," the CUFLA said.

blocks.text: Last year, McGill University cut 25 club and varsity teams across 15 sports, including women’s rugby.
Concordia is now the only English-language university with a varsity women’s rugby team in Quebec.
